title: Angles, and the Nim secret earned
summary: Tear the corners off triangles until angle sums are yours, then the lock from week 2 finally opens: piles into binary, powers into pairs, the copycat unmasked, and counting begins with choices that multiply.
materials: scissors, paper and a ruler for the torn corners

problems.prompt: Shopping week begins, so warm up on sizes. About how many LEGO bricks would fill a shoebox to the top?
explanation: Guess and round: find the box's space, find one brick's space, and divide.
A shoebox is about 30 cm long, 20 cm wide and 10 cm tall, so it holds about 6,000 little cubic centimeters.
A standard brick is about 3 cm by 1.5 cm by 1 cm, which is about 5 cubic centimeters.
6,000 divided by 5 is about 1,200, so about 1,000 bricks is the closest guess.
problems.useAgain: when a container's count is too big to see and you can compare its space with the space one thing takes.
hints: Estimate the shoebox first: about how long, how wide, how tall in centimeters?
Now estimate the space one brick takes, and ask how many of those fit into the box's space.
problems.socraticHint: What two sizes would you need to know before any dividing can even start?

variant.prompt: About how many dice would fill a cereal bowl to the top?

problems.prompt: About how many pennies together weigh as much as you do?
explanation: Guess and round: one penny weighs about 2 and a half grams, roughly two paper clips.
A 9 year old weighs about 30 kilograms, and 30 kilograms is 30,000 grams.
30,000 divided by 2.5 is 12,000, so about 10,000 pennies is the closest guess.
problems.useAgain: when a huge weight can be measured in copies of a tiny thing whose weight you roughly know.
hints: Start tiny: about how many grams does one penny weigh? A paper clip is about a gram.
Turn your own weight into grams, then ask how many penny-weights fit into it.
problems.socraticHint: Why does the final guess barely move if a penny turns out to weigh 2 grams instead of 3?

variant.prompt: About how many grapes together weigh as much as a small child?

problems.prompt: A hardware store sells small screws in a box marked 250 grams. About how many screws are inside?
explanation: Guess and round: a small screw weighs about a gram, the weight of a paper clip.
The box holds 250 grams of them.
250 grams at about a gram each is about 250 screws. Stores sell tiny parts by weight because nobody wants to count them one by one.
problems.useAgain: when things are sold by weight and you want the count without counting.
hints: Hold one small screw in your mind. Is it closer to a gram, ten grams, or a hundred grams? Compare it with a paper clip.
Divide the box's grams by one screw's grams, keeping everything round.
problems.socraticHint: Why would a store print the weight on the box instead of the count?

variant.prompt: A box of small nails is marked 1 kilogram. About how many nails are inside?

problem.prompt: Spatial opener for scissors week: picture a square sheet of paper. One straight snip cuts off exactly one corner, and the cut piece falls away. How many corners does the sheet have now? See it in your head first; the real snip is for checking afterwards.
explanation: Fold it in your head: run the scissors line across one corner before any real cut.
The snip removes 1 old corner, but the cut line touches two sides of the square, and each touching point becomes a brand new corner.
So the count goes 4, minus the 1 that fell away, plus the 2 the cut made: 5 corners.
Snip a real square to check: the sheet in your hand now has five sides and five corners.
problem.useAgain: when a cut or fold changes a shape and you need to track what disappears and what gets created.
hints: The snip takes one corner away. But look at where the cut line starts and ends: what does each end of the cut become?
Count what is lost and what is gained separately, then put the two counts together.
problem.socraticHint: Can a straight cut remove something from a shape's outline without adding anything new to it?

variant.prompt: Picture a square sheet of paper. Two straight snips each cut off one corner, different corners, and both pieces fall away. How many corners does the sheet have now? Sketch it on graph paper if your head wants help.

problems.prompt: Meet the protractor: a half circle of degree marks, 0 to 180 along its straight edge. A square corner, like the corner of this page, measures exactly 90 degrees. An angle opened a little wider than a square corner measures about which of these?
explanation: Guess and round before you measure: park the angle between landmarks you know.
A square corner is 90 degrees, and a straight line is 180 degrees, the protractor's whole straight edge.
A little wider than 90 but nowhere near flat lands at 110 degrees. 60 is narrower than a square corner, and 180 is no corner at all.
Estimate first every time you measure: the guess catches you if you ever read the protractor's wrong scale.
problems.useAgain: when a measurement needs a rough guess first so a silly reading cannot sneak past you.
hints: Two landmark angles anchor everything: the square corner at 90 and the straight line at 180. Where between them does this angle sit?
Cross off every option that is not wider than a square corner, then every option that is nearly flat.
problems.socraticHint: Before reading any scale, what two angles do you already know by sight that could fence this one in?

variant.prompt: A square corner measures 90 degrees. An angle a little narrower than a square corner measures about which of these?

problems.prompt: The discovery. Draw any triangle on paper, long and thin or short and fat, your choice. Cut it out, tear off its three corners, and lay the torn corners point to point along the edge of a ruler. Together the three corners exactly fill up which of these?
options: a half turn, a straight line of 180 degrees
explanation: Corners on a line: tear the corners off and let them confess together.
The three points meet at one spot and their edges fan out until the two outer edges lie flat along the ruler: a straight line, no gap, no overlap.
A straight line is half a full turn, 180 degrees, the protractor's whole straight edge.
Tear up a second, completely different triangle and it happens again. Every triangle's three angles add to 180 degrees, and your hands found it before anyone told you.
problems.useAgain: when a shape's angles need adding and a straight line or a full turn can hold them for you.
hints: Actually do the tearing, do not just imagine it. Lay the three points together at one spot on the ruler's edge.
Look at the two outside edges of your fan of corners: what one flat thing do they line up with?
problems.socraticHint: If a skinny triangle and a fat triangle both fill the same amount, what must be true about every triangle's three corners together?

variant.prompt: Draw any four-sided shape on paper, cut it out, tear off its four corners, and lay them point to point around one dot on the page. Together the four torn corners exactly fill up which of these?

problems.prompt:
Sana found the missing angle on a straight line where one angle measures 112 degrees.
Line 1: A straight line holds exactly 180 degrees total.
Line 2: The two angles on the line must add up to 180 degrees.
Line 3: 180 minus 112 is 78.
Line 4: So the missing angle is 78 degrees.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Lines 1 and 2 are correct: a straight line holds 180 degrees, split between the two angles.
Line 3 is wrong: 180 minus 112 is 68, not 78.
Corners on a line: the two angles must fill the line together, so subtracting one from 180 finds the other.
The missing angle is really 68 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when a straight line's two angles are set up correctly but the subtraction still needs its own check.
hints: Do not assume any line is correct just because the ones before it look fine. Recompute each line yourself, including which total the angles are supposed to add up to.
Corners on a line: two angles sharing a straight line always add up to exactly 180 degrees, not 90.
problems.socraticHint: How many degrees does a straight line hold in total, and does the working actually use that number?

variant.prompt:
Malik found the missing angle on a straight line where one angle measures 65 degrees.
Line 1: A straight line holds exactly 180 degrees total.
Line 2: Since a square corner is 90 degrees and this split looks about that size, use 90 degrees as the total instead.
Line 3: 90 minus 65 is 25.
Line 4: So the missing angle is 25 degrees.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: A triangle has a square corner of exactly 90 degrees, and one more angle of 35 degrees. How many degrees is the third angle?
explanation: Corners on a line: your torn corners proved every triangle's three angles add to 180 degrees.
90 plus 35 is 125 already spent.
180 minus 125 leaves 55 for the third corner.
problems.useAgain: when two of a triangle's angles are known and the 180 total hands you the third.
hints: What did the three torn corners of every triangle add up to on the ruler's edge?
Add the two angles you know, then see what is left of that total.
problems.socraticHint: What total do all three angles have to share, no matter what this triangle looks like?

variant.prompt: A triangle has a square corner of exactly 90 degrees, and one more angle of 62 degrees. How many degrees is the third angle?

problems.prompt: A triangle has angles of 62 degrees and 49 degrees. How many degrees is the third angle? Draw it with your protractor afterwards and measure, to catch the paper agreeing with the arithmetic.
explanation: Corners on a line: 180 degrees for the three together, always.
62 plus 49 is 111.
180 minus 111 leaves 69.
The protractor check may land a degree off, and that is honest: hand drawing wobbles, the sum does not.
problems.useAgain: when two angles are known in any triangle, square corner or not.
hints: The same 180 total works for every triangle, not only ones with a square corner in them.
Add the two known angles first, carefully: 62 plus 49 crosses a ten.
problems.socraticHint: Does the 180 rule care whether one of the angles happens to be 90?

variant.prompt: A triangle has angles of 57 degrees and 46 degrees. How many degrees is the third angle?

problems.prompt: A four-sided shape has angles of 90 degrees, 80 degrees and 120 degrees. How many degrees is the fourth angle?
explanation: Corners on a line, full turn edition: the four torn corners of any four-sided shape fill a whole turn, 360 degrees.
You can also see it with a diagonal: one straight cut corner to corner splits the shape into two triangles, and two triangles carry 180 plus 180.
90 plus 80 plus 120 is 290.
360 minus 290 leaves 70.
problems.useAgain: when a four-sided shape's angles need the full turn's 360 to give up the missing one.
hints: Suppose you tore the corners off a four-sided scrap and laid them point to point around one dot. What would they close up into, and how many degrees is that?
Add the three known angles, then subtract from the whole turn.
problems.socraticHint: What happens to a four-sided shape when one straight cut runs corner to corner, and what does that say about its angle total?

variant.prompt: A four-sided shape has angles of 100 degrees, 95 degrees and 75 degrees. How many degrees is the fourth angle?

problems.prompt: A builder's puzzle, the kind your free build plan may meet this very week. A ramp leans against a wall that stands perfectly straight up from flat ground. The ramp makes a 25 degree angle with the ground. How many degrees is the angle between the ramp and the wall?
explanation: Corners on a line: the ground, the wall and the ramp close up into a triangle, so its three angles share 180 degrees.
The wall meets the flat ground in a square corner: 90 degrees.
90 plus 25 is 115, and 180 minus 115 leaves 65 between the ramp and the wall.
Real plans hide triangles everywhere: find the triangle, and two known corners always pay for the third.
problems.useAgain: when a plan's slanted part meets flat and upright parts and the hidden triangle gives the angle for free.
hints: Sketch it small: flat ground, upright wall, slanted ramp. What closed shape do the three make?
One of the triangle's angles is where wall meets ground. What must that one measure?
problems.socraticHint: Which of the three corners in your sketch do you already know without measuring anything?

variant.prompt: A ramp leans against a wall that stands perfectly straight up from flat ground. The ramp makes a 38 degree angle with the ground. How many degrees is the angle between the ramp and the wall?

steps.title: One corner cut away, and a tally that will not sit still

problems.prompt: A patio is an 8 m by 5 m rectangle with a 3 m by 2 m rectangular pond cut from one corner (shown shaded). What is the patio's area, not counting the pond, in square meters?
explanation: The full rectangle is 8 times 5, which is 40 square meters.
The pond removes 3 times 2, which is 6 square meters.
40 minus 6 is 34 square meters.
problems.useAgain: when a real shape like a patio or floor has a rectangular piece missing that needs subtracting from the whole.
hints: Work out the full rectangle's area, pond included, first.
Subtract the pond's own rectangular area from that total.
problems.socraticHint: Does the pond count toward the patio's usable area, or does it need to come out of the total?

figure.alt: An 8 by 5 grid of squares with the top-right 3 by 2 block of squares left unshaded, showing the patio with the pond's corner removed.

variant.prompt: A patio is a 9 m by 6 m rectangle with a 4 m by 2 m rectangular pond cut from one corner. What is the patio's area, not counting the pond, in square meters?

problems.prompt: A patio is a 7 m by 6 m rectangle with a 3 m by 4 m rectangular pond cut from one corner (shown shaded). What is the patio's area, not counting the pond, in square meters?
explanation: The full rectangle is 7 times 6, which is 42 square meters.
The pond removes 3 times 4, which is 12 square meters.
42 minus 12 is 30 square meters.
problems.useAgain: when a bigger missing piece needs subtracting, checking that its own two side lengths are multiplied correctly first.
hints: Find the full rectangle's area before anything is removed.
Multiply the pond's two side lengths, then subtract that from the full area.
problems.socraticHint: Does the order you multiply the pond's two side lengths in change how big the missing piece is?

figure.alt: A 7 by 6 grid of squares with the top-right 3 by 4 block of squares left unshaded, showing the patio with the pond's corner removed.

variant.prompt: A patio is an 8 m by 6 m rectangle with a 2 m by 5 m rectangular pond cut from one corner. What is the patio's area, not counting the pond, in square meters?

problems.prompt: A fair die is rolled 30 times. The tally shows a 6 came up 3 times. How many fewer times than the expected count of 5 did a 6 actually come up?
explanation: Over 30 rolls, a fair die is expected to land on 6 about 5 times.
The real tally shows only 3, which is 2 less than expected.
A short run like this wobbling below the expected count does not mean the die is unfair.
problems.useAgain: when a real tally comes out lower or higher than the expected long-run count, and the gap itself is what is asked for.
hints: What count would you expect a 6 to reach over 30 rolls?
Subtract the real tally from that expected count.
problems.socraticHint: Does landing below the expected count in one run of 30 rolls prove anything is wrong with the die?

variant.prompt: A fair die is rolled 30 times. The tally shows a 6 came up 9 times. How many more times than the expected count of 5 did a 6 actually come up?

problems.prompt: In that same 30-roll tally, a 3 came up 7 times. How many more times than the expected count of 5 did a 3 actually come up?
explanation: The expected count for any single number over 30 rolls is still 5.
The real tally shows 7, which is 2 more than expected.
Different numbers can wobble above or below the expected count in the very same 30 rolls.
problems.useAgain: when comparing a different face's real tally to the same expected count, in the same run of rolls.
hints: What is the expected count for any one number over 30 rolls?
Subtract the expected count from the real tally.
problems.socraticHint: Can two different numbers wobble in opposite directions from the expected count within the very same 30 rolls?

variant.prompt: In that same 30-roll tally, a 2 came up 2 times. How many fewer times than the expected count of 5 did a 2 actually come up?

steps.title: The Nim payoff, then counting begins

problems.prompt: Seven weeks ago the copycat trick met piles it could not crack, and you were promised the full secret needed two machine parts: week 2's binary, and week 3's XOR, the difference detector. Today the lock opens. Piles of 5, 4 and 1, last counter wins. Write each pile as a binary row: 5 is 101, 4 is 100, 1 is 001. Stack the rows and look down each column: the fours column holds two 1s, the twos column none, the ones column two. Every column holds an even count, every power has its twin: call that balanced. True or false: whatever move the next player makes from 5, 4 and 1, the position they leave behind must be unbalanced.
explanation: Binary balance: write each pile in binary and pair up the powers across the piles.
A move shrinks exactly one pile, so exactly one binary row changes, and a changed number must differ from the old row in at least one column.
One changed row flips that column's count between even and odd, so at least one column goes odd: the balance breaks, every time, whatever they take.
This is week 3's XOR doing the judging: a column is quiet when its 1s pair off and cries out when one stands alone. XOR every row together and a balanced position answers all zeros.
So balanced spots are the doomed spots, exactly like the multiples of 4 in the 21 game: every exit from one lands in trouble. The next problem shows the trouble can always be handed straight back.
problems.useAgain: when a pile game position needs judging: write the piles in binary and ask whether every power has its twin.
hints: A move touches exactly one pile. Write that pile's binary row before and after some take you choose, and compare the two rows column by column.
Ask what happens to one column's count of 1s when exactly one of its rows changes.
problems.socraticHint: Can a pile change size without its binary row changing in at least one column?

variant.prompt: Piles of 6, 5 and 3, last counter wins. In binary: 6 is 110, 5 is 101, 3 is 011. Stack the rows: the fours column holds two 1s, the twos column two, the ones column two. Every power has its twin, so the position is balanced. True or false: the next player has at least one move that leaves another balanced position behind.

problems.prompt: Now the other half of the secret: from an unbalanced position, some move always rebalances, and that move is the winning move. Piles of 2, 5 and 6, your turn, last counter wins. In binary: 2 is 010, 5 is 101, 6 is 110. The fours column pairs, the twos column pairs, but the ones column holds a single lonely 1. Which move hands your opponent a balanced position?
options: Take 1 from the pile of 5, leaving 2, 4 and 6
Take 2 from the pile of 6, leaving 2, 5 and 4
Take the whole pile of 2, leaving 5 and 6
explanation: Binary balance: the lonely 1 sits in the ones column of the 5, so the 5 is the pile to fix.
Take 1 from it: 2, 4 and 6 are 010, 100 and 110, and now the fours pair, the twos pair and the ones column is empty. Balanced, and your opponent inherits the doom.

Check the others with your counters. 2, 5 and 4 leaves the twos column with a lonely 1. And 5 and 6 are unequal piles, which copycat week taught you to distrust: 101 and 110 leave the twos and the ones columns both odd.
One move rebalances, the rest hand the game away. Set out the counters and play it, and feel the trap close from the right side.
problems.useAgain: when it is your move in a pile game and the lonely, unpaired power tells you which pile to shrink and by how much.
hints: Find the column where a 1 stands without a twin. Which pile put it there?
Shrink that pile to a number whose binary row makes every column pair up again. Write candidate rows and check the columns.
problems.socraticHint: Which single pile could change so the lonely column evens out while the paired columns stay paired?

variant.prompt: Piles of 1, 2 and 4, your turn, last counter wins. In binary: 001, 010, 100. Every column holds a single lonely 1, so the position is wildly unbalanced. Which move hands your opponent a balanced position?
options: Take the whole pile of 1, leaving 2 and 4
Take 1 from the pile of 2, leaving 1, 1 and 4
Take 1 from the pile of 4, leaving 1, 2 and 3

problems.prompt:
Priya tried to prove that a balanced pile of stones always loses for whoever moves next.
Line 1: I checked the pile 5, 4, 1. In binary that is 101, 100, 001, and counting each column: the fours column has two, the twos column has zero, and the ones column has two. All even, so it pairs evenly.
Line 2: I checked the pile 6, 5, 3. In binary that is 110, 101, 011, and counting each column: the fours column has two, the twos column has two, and the ones column has two. All even, so it pairs evenly.
Line 3: I checked the pile 7, 7. In binary that is 111, 111; every column has two 1s, all even, so it pairs evenly.
Line 4: Every balanced pile I checked lost for whoever moved next, so every balanced pile there is must also lose for whoever moves next.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Lines 1 to 3 correctly check that 5, 4, 1 and 6, 5, 3 and 7, 7 all pair evenly in every column.
Line 4 is wrong: three checked piles can never guarantee every other pile behaves the same way, since an untried pile could be the exception.
A real proof has to argue about every possible pile at once.
For example, it could show any single move can only ever break one column's pairing, never all of them.
Checking examples is a great way to find the pattern, but only a general argument like that can prove it always holds.
problems.useAgain: when a rule has only ever been checked on a few examples and you want to remember that checking is not the same as proving.
hints: Recompute every line yourself, including whether each column-count claimed is really even or really odd.
Checking examples, no matter how carefully, is a different thing from proving a rule holds for every case there could ever be.
problems.socraticHint: If Priya had checked ten piles instead of three, would that turn her checking into a real proof?

variant.prompt:
Marisol checked whether the pile 4, 6 is balanced.
Line 1: 4 in binary is 100, and 6 in binary is 110.
Line 2: Stack them: the fours column has a 1 from each number, two 1s in total.
Line 3: The twos column has a 1 only from 6, one 1 in total, and the ones column has no 1s from either number, zero in total.
Line 4: Two, one and zero are all even numbers, so every column pairs evenly and the pile 4, 6 is balanced.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: A bike lock has 3 rings, and each ring shows one digit from 0 to 9. How many different codes can the lock hold?
explanation: Choices multiply: when choices stack, multiply the ways.
The first ring has 10 ways to sit. For every one of those, the second ring has its own 10 ways: 10 x 10 is 100 ways for two rings.
Each of those 100 splits ten ways again on the third ring: 10 x 10 x 10 is 1,000.
You met this move in week 1 with buttons: each button doubled the patterns. Rings multiply by 10 instead of 2, and the codes run from 000 up to 999, which really is 1,000 numbers.
problems.useAgain: when stacked choices are each free to be anything, and the total count comes from multiplying instead of listing.
hints: Start with a one-ring lock: how many codes? Now add a second ring: what happens to each of those codes?
Every ring you add takes every code you already have and splits it into 10 new ones.
problems.socraticHint: Why does a new ring multiply the count instead of just adding 10 more codes?

variant.prompt: A lock has 4 rings, and each ring shows one digit from 0 to 9. How many different codes can the lock hold?

problems.prompt: A sandwich cart offers 4 breads, 3 fillings and 2 sauces. A sandwich is one bread, one filling and one sauce. How many different sandwiches can the cart make?
explanation: Choices multiply: bread, then filling, then sauce, each choice free of the others.
4 breads times 3 fillings is 12 bread-and-filling pairs.
Each of the 12 pairs takes either sauce: 12 x 2 is 24.
Draw the tree on graph paper if you want to see it breathe: 4 branches, each splitting in 3, each of those splitting in 2.
problems.useAgain: when a menu of independent picks needs counting and listing every combination would take all day.
hints: Count the bread-and-filling pairs first, ignoring sauce completely.
Now each of those pairs can finish two ways. What does that do to the pair count?
problems.socraticHint: Does picking a bread change how many fillings are still open to you?

variant.prompt: A snack cart offers 5 breads, 2 fillings and 3 sauces. A snack is one bread, one filling and one sauce. How many different snacks can the cart make?

problems.prompt: Your micro:bit's display is a 5 by 5 grid of lights, 25 in all, and each light is either on or off. Every pattern of ons and offs is one badge picture. About how many different badge pictures can the display show?
explanation: Choices multiply: 25 lights, each with 2 ways, so the count is 2 multiplied by itself 25 times, which exponents write as 2 to the power 25.
Climb it in jumps: 2 to the 10th is 1,024, about a thousand. So 2 to the 20th is about a thousand thousands, a million.
Five doublings remain: 2 to the 5th is 32, and 32 times a million is about 33 million. The exact count is 33,554,432.
That is why nobody will ever see all the badge pictures: at one per second it would take more than a year without sleeping. Small choices, multiplied, build monstrous counts.
problems.useAgain: when each of many spots has a few ways and you want to feel how fast the total explodes.
hints: One light has 2 ways. Two lights have 4. How many multiplications by 2 does the whole grid take?
Use the week 1 ladder: 2 to the 10th is about a thousand. Stack those jumps until you reach 25 doublings.
problems.socraticHint: What does every single light do to the count of pictures, no matter how many lights came before it?

variant.prompt: A little badge is a 4 by 4 grid of lights, 16 in all, each on or off. About how many different pictures can it show?

problems.prompt: A tiny town is 2 blocks by 2 blocks, so its streets draw a grid of 9 corners. Home is the top left corner and the park is the bottom right. Walking only rightward or downward along the streets, how many different routes lead from home to the park?
explanation: Careful: these choices tangle. Every route spends exactly 2 rights and 2 downs, so a right spent early is a right you no longer have late. Multiplying 2 choices at every step gives 16, counting walks that march off the edge of town.
When choices tangle, add the ways corner by corner instead. Write 1 at every corner along the top edge and the left edge: one way to each, straight along.
Every other corner is reached from above or from the left, so its ways are those two numbers added. Fill the grid and the counts grow until the park corner collects 3 plus 3.
That is 6 routes. Check by listing the orders of 2 rights and 2 downs: RRDD, RDRD, RDDR, DRRD, DRDR, DDRR, six exactly.
Keep this grid in your pocket: week 11 brings it back wearing a famous name.
problems.useAgain: when the ways to reach a spot come from adding the ways to reach the spots just before it.
hints: Try the smallest town first: 1 block by 1 block. Trace every route with your finger and count them.
Label each corner with the number of routes that reach it, starting along the two edges. Where can a walker standing at any corner have just come from?
problems.socraticHint: Why does multiplying work for the lock's rings but overcount the town's routes? What is different about these choices?

variant.prompt: A strip of town is 2 blocks wide and 1 block tall, so its streets draw a grid of 6 corners. Home is the top left corner and the park is the bottom right. Walking only rightward or downward along the streets, how many different routes lead from home to the park?

steps.title: Explain it in writing
steps.prompt: Write the letter week 2 could not write: to the you who only knew the copycat trick, explain the full Nim secret, one idea per sentence: how a pile becomes a binary row, what pairing the powers means, why a balanced position is doomed, and why twin piles were balanced all along. Name the idea you used.

steps.title: Explain back
steps.prompt: Set out piles of 3, 5 and 6 tonight and play the pile game against a grown-up, letting them move first, best of three. Before each of your moves, check the balance on paper and rebalance. Then record yourself explaining how the game felt from the winning side: what you checked on each turn, and how the copycat trick turned out to be one small case of the balance test. Then invent one new pile-taking rule of your own, and write its winning-position pattern for a sibling to check.
